nameStory: The name 'mullein foxglove' comes from the plant's resemblance to two other well-known wildflowers. Its tall, fuzzy stems and leaves remind people of common mullein, while its tubular yellow flowers are shaped like those of a foxglove. It's like nature created a mashup of two familiar plants!
description: Mullein foxglove is a towering wildflower that can reach up to six feet tall, making it hard to miss in the forest. This impressive plant produces bright yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers that bloom in summer along its tall stems. It's typically a short-lived plant, usually lasting just one or two years before completing its life cycle. Despite its height, it has a somewhat delicate appearance with its slender stems and scattered blooms.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow tubular flowers shaped like tiny trumpets, blooming scattered along the upper portions of the tall stems in summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Exceptionally tall for a wildflower, reaching up to 6 feet in height with a single main stem that towers above most other woodland plants

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large leaves that feel somewhat fuzzy to the touch, arranged alternately along the stem and decreasing in size toward the top

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy stem that feels slightly hairy when touched and can support the plant's impressive height without major branching

habitat: Look for mullein foxglove in dry to moderately dry woodlands, especially on limestone-rich soils or rocky bluffs. In New England, this is an extremely rare find, as the species mainly grows west of the Appalachian Mountains. When present, it prefers undisturbed forest areas with good drainage and calcareous (calcium-rich) soil conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the plant begins its dramatic upward climb, with large basal leaves forming first before the stem starts to elongate.
seasonality.summer: The spectacular bloom period when bright yellow tubular flowers appear along the towering stems, making the plant impossible to miss in the woodland.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, while the tall dried stems may persist for a while before the annual or biennial plant completes its life cycle.
seasonality.winter: Usually absent, as most plants are annual or biennial, though occasionally dried stems from the previous year may still be visible as skeletal remains.

funFact: This towering wildflower is actually a sneaky thief! Mullein foxglove is hemiparasitic, meaning it taps into the roots of nearby trees and shrubs to steal water and nutrients while still doing some of its own photosynthesis - like having a part-time job while also pickpocketing your neighbors.
confusionNotes: The yellow tubular flowers and extreme height make this distinctive from most plants, but it could potentially be confused with other tall yellow-flowered plants like wild parsnip or goldenrod. However, mullein foxglove's trumpet-shaped individual flowers and woodland habitat set it apart from these meadow species with their clustered tiny flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, mullein foxglove isn't closely related to either true mullein (Verbascum) or true foxgloves (Digitalis). It was recently moved from the figwort family to the broomrape family based on DNA studies, reflecting our evolving understanding of plant relationships.
compareHints: Mullein foxglove is the only species in its genus Dasistoma, making it truly unique. Within the broomrape family, it differs from other members by being much taller and having yellow flowers, while most of its relatives are smaller parasitic plants with purple, white, or brownish flowers. Its combination of great height, yellow trumpet flowers, and woodland habitat makes it unmistakable among New England's broomrape family members.
